title: Ten years on, is the UK preparing to undo Brexit? | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

Leaders from theUnited Kingdomand European Union have reached what’s been hailed as a “win-win” deal, in a summit held as British Prime MinisterAndy Burnhampushes for a closer relationship with the bloc a decade after the Brexit vote.

A new package of agreements to create new opportunities for young people to live, study and travel on the continent, link emissions trading, and remove trade barriers on food products has been agreed, a UK government spokesperson told CNN on Friday.

Burnham welcomed the “landmark” deal, saying it draws a line “on a decade of drift and division by reconnecting with old friends.”

“We’re 10 years on from Brexit, but I think we can all confidently say this is a good day for Britain, and this is a good day for Europe. The agreement that we’ve reached together is a win-win,” he said at a news conference following the Brussels summit.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen set out a range of areas for further collaboration on economic security, defense capabilities, artificial intelligence and illegal immigration.

She said the deal marked a “turning point” in UK-EU relations, Britain’s Press Association news agency reported.

After Friday’s negotiations concluded, the UK government spokesperson said both sides would work toward the implementation of the schemes. The spokesperson added that talks would continue “on some areas,” alluding to key sticking points which remain.

Britain’s center-left Labour government inherited Brexit from its predecessors, the Conservative Party, and has long spoken of “resetting” ties with Brussels.

But in the four months since he became prime minister, Burnham has staked out a more bullish position on Europe, appearing willing to revisit the politically charged Brexit debate and take on the right-wing parties that fiercely oppose reversing 2016’s referendum result and reestablishing closer ties with Europe.

Last month, he even said he’d like to see Britain rejoin the bloc in his lifetime but ruled that out in this parliament, alongside crossing his party’s “red lines” from their 2024 manifesto of returning to the single market or customs union, or restoring freedom of movement.

Nonetheless, he committed to beginning talks with the EU “about options for our long-term relationship” after Friday’s summit without providing further details or timeline.

Economists broadly agree thatleaving the EU stymied the UK’s economic growthpotential – with estimates ranging from 2% to as much as 8% of foregone output. So as the government scrabbles for levers to kickstart economic growth, the EU, as Britain’s biggest trading partner and neighbor, has become part of the conversation.

Following Labour’s election in 2024 under Burnham’s predecessor Keir Starmer, it promised to “make Brexit work.” Starmer’s strategy was to reboot the UK-EU relationship by negotiating limited deals and aligning some regulations to ease trade frictions.

But Starmer’s technocratic, cautious approach – on Europe and other policy areas – led in large part to his party ousting him this summer. The more confident, media-savvy Burnham emerged in his place.

Friday’s summit was largely a product of Starmer’s approach, originally scheduled for earlier this year but delayed when his premiership imploded.

Nick Thomas-Symonds, a member of parliament who served as Europe minister under Starmer, told CNN the deal was “90% there” when Burnham’s team took over.

Even after the summit, sticking points remain, including whether tuition fees for EU students studying at UK universities will be aligned with those of their British counterparts. European Council President António Costa shied away from directly answering a question about whether the deals announced today are contingent on the UK agreeing to lower tuition fees for European students.

A joint EU-UK statement released Friday said the parties would work toward a “supplementing agreement” on tuition fees, with negotiations expected to conclude within six months.

The youth scheme, which will allow 100,000 young people from the EU and the UK respectively to live for up to three years for work, studies or traveling, is expected to be available no later than January 2030, the statement said.

Burnham’s rhetoric on Europe has been more forceful, but his actual approach hasn’t changed “an iota” from Starmer’s, said Anand Menon, a professor at King’s College London and director of the think-tank UK in a Changing Europe, in comments to CNN ahead of the summit.

“The only difference is how we talk about the future, and Burnham saying we might consider rejoining,” he said. “The more people talk about rejoining, the more obviously complicated an undertaking it becomes. I don’t know where Burnham goes on this.”

Further changes in the UK-EU relationship are unlikely, Menon added, unless the government compromises on its “red lines.”

His assessment echoes that of the EU’s former Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier, who warned earlier this month that the UK cannot “cherry pick” certain elements of the single market.

For his part, Thomas-Symonds pointed to more cooperation on immigration, stronger military ties and aligning regulations in other sectors as ways to deepen ties with the EU without breaking party promises. “Obviously, these bigger points are ones that we’re looking at in the next manifesto,” he said.

Even Burnham himself acknowledged that Friday’s agreement is “probably the limit of what we can achieve in this parliament.”

Burnham’s ambitious rhetoric has shifted the political conversation, however. Two campaign groups – both with ties to the original “Vote Leave” campaign – either launched or rebranded this week with the express purpose of opposing any attempts to rejoin the EU.

Conservative opposition leader Kemi Badenoch, meanwhile, accused Burnham of having “not learnt the lessons of the past,” arguing that “the problems this country faces today have nothing to do with being in or out of the EU.” Brexit architect Nigel Farage, who leads the hard-right Reform UK party, said that Burnham “has no mandate” to negotiate closer ties with Brussels.

Notwithstanding the Euroskeptic right flank, who are unlikely ever to vote for Labour, the politics of promising to rejoin the EU might actually be favorable for Burnham, noted Morgan Jones, deputy director of Persuasion UK, an organization that researches public opinion.

Polling suggests that if “there were an option to rejoin on 2016 terms tomorrow, it would be resoundingly popular,” she told CNN, saying that it also appeals to the different voters Labour would need to win a parliamentary majority.

But the same cannot be said of the process of actually doing so, she added. “We found that people were put off by the prospect of budget contributions or any threat of joining the Euro and also simply by the process itself – there is significant voter exhaustion on this topic,” she said, citing research Persuasion conducted with a pro-EU think tank.

Until now, the “reset” has yielded few tangible outcomes aside from an agreement for Britainto rejoin the Erasmus student exchange programnext year, at a much higher cost than before.

Burnham says these agreements could add up to 0.5% of GDP to the British economy and remove bureaucratic hurdles for food exporters.

But Europe Minister Hamish Falconer conceded to the BBC that their implementation would compel the UK to accept EU regulations on products without being able to shape them.

It echoes the old trade-off – sovereignty versus frictionless trade – which underpinned the fractious years-long Brexit debate, the legacy of which hangs over whatever Burnham’s government decides to do next and Europe’s own moves.

Indeed, the bloc’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said last week that the EU had suffered “a lot of trauma” from Britain’s departure before warning that any future negotiations “will not be that easy.”
